\chapter{Thank You, Yes, and No}
\label{ch:thank-you}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can thank someone, answer when I am thanked, and say yes or no.}

Thanks, the answer to thanks, and the two words that let you accept or decline.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sí]{sí — yes}

\label{lesson:ES-C19-si}



\begin{quote}
The smallest useful word — and the accent on it is doing real work.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sí} = \textbf{yes}. One syllable, said \emph{see}.

The written accent is not decoration — it is the \textbf{whole difference} between two words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{sí} (with the accent) = \textbf{yes}
  \item \textbf{si} (no accent) = \textbf{if}
\end{itemize}

They sound almost identical, so Spanish uses the mark to tell them apart on the page: \emph{Sí, si quieres} = \textquotedblleft{}Yes, if you want.\textquotedblright{} Miss the accent and you've written \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{} where you meant \textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sí} is Latin \textbf{sīc}, \textquotedblleft{}thus, so\textquotedblright{} — answering a question with \textquotedblleft{}just so,\textquotedblright{} exactly the move Latin also made with \textbf{ita} (\textquotedblleft{}thus\textquotedblright{} = yes, from the Latin yes/no lesson). Its Romance cousins kept the same root:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin \emph{sīc}} & \textbf{$\to$} \\
\midrule
Spanish & \textbf{sí} \\
Italian & \textbf{sì} \\
Portuguese & \textbf{sim} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

French is the odd one out — it went a completely different way for \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} (\emph{oui}), which its own lesson tells. But say \emph{sí, sì, sim} in a row and you hear one Latin word answering across three countries.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sí\textquotedblright{} — \emph{see}, and picture the accent
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}sí\textquotedblright{} (yes) vs \textquotedblleft{}si\textquotedblright{} (if)
  \item the cousins — \textquotedblleft{}sí, sì, sim\textquotedblright{} — all from Latin \emph{sīc}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say yes in Spanish? (\textbf{sí}.) What is the \emph{only} difference between \textbf{sí} \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{si} \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{}? (The \textbf{written accent}.) What Latin word is \emph{sí} from, and what did it mean? (\textbf{sīc} — \textquotedblleft{}thus, so\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[no]{no — no / not}

\label{lesson:ES-C19-no}



\begin{quote}
The easiest word yet — and it quietly does two jobs Spanish never splits apart.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{no} = \textbf{no}. Said \emph{noh}, a clean single vowel.

It is Latin \textbf{nōn} with almost nothing worn off — just the final consonant gone. Compare the family, all from the same \emph{nōn}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin \emph{nōn}} & \textbf{$\to$} \\
\midrule
Spanish & \textbf{no} \\
Italian & \textbf{no} \\
French & \textbf{non} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's the thing English splits and Spanish doesn't. English has \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}} (the answer) and \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}} (inside a sentence) — two different words. Spanish uses \textbf{no} for \textbf{both}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item as the \textbf{answer}. Someone asks you something — anything at all — and this one syllable declines it. You do not need to understand the question to answer it, which is exactly why this word comes early.
  \item and later, as the word that turns a sentence around — but that needs a sentence first, so it waits until you have one. For now: \emph{\textbf{no}} is how you decline, refuse, and disagree, which is most of what a beginner needs it for.
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} — \emph{noh}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}No.\textquotedblright{} — flat, once, the way you would decline a second coffee
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Sí.\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}No.\textquotedblright{} — the two shortest complete answers in Spanish
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say no in Spanish? (\textbf{no}.) What Latin word is it from? (\textbf{nōn}.) Spanish \emph{no} does the work of which \textbf{two} English words? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}} the answer, and later the word for \textquotedblleft{}not.\textquotedblright{}) Where does \emph{no} go to negate a sentence? (\textbf{Right before the verb}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gracias]{gracias — \textquotedblleft{}thank you,\textquotedblright{} and a whole family of English words}

\label{lesson:ES-C04-gracias}



\begin{quote}
You can now introduce yourself. The next exchange is \emph{how are you?} — but every answer ends the same polite way, so we learn the courtesy word first: \textbf{gracias}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-a} — the clean \emph{ah} of \emph{father}, twice.
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — a single flicked \emph{r} (not the English one, and not yet the rolled \emph{rr}): the tongue taps once, like the middle of American \emph{butter}.
  \item \texttt{ci-th-s} — the \emph{ci} is a soft \emph{s} in Latin America (\textbf{GRAH-syahs}) and a soft \emph{th} in most of Spain (\textbf{GRAH-thyahs}). Either is correct — pick one.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gracias} is the plural of \textbf{gracia} (\textquotedblleft{}grace, favour\textquotedblright{}), from Latin \textbf{grātia} — \emph{favour freely given}. Saying \emph{gracias} literally offers someone \textquotedblleft{}graces,\textquotedblright{} i.e. good will in return for theirs.

That one Latin root \textbf{grātia} fans out across English — once you see it, you get a fistful of words for free:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{grace}, \textbf{gracious}, \textbf{graceful} — the direct borrowings.
  \item \textbf{grateful}, \textbf{gratitude} — being \emph{full of} grātia.
  \item \textbf{gratis}, \textbf{gratuity} — something given as a \emph{favour} (for free, or a tip).
  \item \textbf{congratulate} — literally \textquotedblleft{}to wish grace \emph{together with} someone.\textquotedblright{}
  \item Italian \textbf{grazie}, French \emph{grâces}, Portuguese \emph{graças} — the whole Romance family kept grātia, even where everyday thanks went elsewhere (French says \emph{merci}, Portuguese \emph{obrigado}).
\end{itemize}

So \emph{gracias} is not a word to memorize cold: it is \textbf{grace}, made plural and handed to another person.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gracias\textquotedblright{} — \emph{GRAH-syahs}, one soft tap on the \emph{r}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gracias\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}grace, grateful, gratitude\textquotedblright{} — one family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What everyday English word is \emph{gracias} the plural of, at the root? (\emph{Grace}.) So when you thank someone in Spanish, you are literally handing them — what? (Graces / favours.) Next: the little reply that closes the exchange, \textbf{de nada}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[de nada]{de nada — \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}it was nothing\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C04-de-nada}



\begin{quote}
Someone says \textbf{gracias}. You need the reply that closes the loop: \textbf{de nada} — literally \emph{\textquotedblleft{}of nothing.\textquotedblright{}} You're waving the favour off as no trouble at all — the same move English makes with \emph{\textquotedblleft{}it's nothing\textquotedblright{}} / \emph{\textquotedblleft{}no problem.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{d-soft} — the \emph{d} in \emph{nada} is soft, almost the \emph{th} of \emph{this} (\textbf{NAH-thah}), not a hard English \emph{d}. Spanish \emph{d} between vowels always softens.
  \item \texttt{vowel-a} — three clean \emph{ah} sounds: \emph{deh NAH-thah}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{de} = \textquotedblleft{}of / from\textquotedblright{} (Latin \textbf{dē}) — the same \emph{de} hiding in English \textbf{de}part, \textbf{de}duct, \textbf{de}scend.
  \item \textbf{nada} = \textquotedblleft{}nothing.\textquotedblright{} And this is the beautiful part.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{nada} comes from Latin \textbf{(rēs) nāta} — \textquotedblleft{}(a thing) \emph{born}.\textquotedblright{} From \emph{nāscī}, \textquotedblleft{}to be born,\textquotedblright{} the same root as English \textbf{nat}ive, \textbf{nat}ure, \textbf{nat}al, \textbf{re-nais-sance} (re-birth). Latin speakers said \emph{nōn est rēs nāta}, \textquotedblleft{}there is not a born thing\textquotedblright{} — \emph{not a single thing that ever came into being} — and over centuries the emphatic \emph{nāta} (\textquotedblleft{}born thing\textquotedblright{}) wore down until \textbf{the word for 'born thing' became the word for 'nothing' itself.}

So the reply \emph{de nada} literally says \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}of {[}a{]} born-thing\textquotedblright{}} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}of nothing at all.\textquotedblright{} French did the identical trick with \textbf{rien} (\textquotedblleft{}nothing\textquotedblright{}) — which is Latin \textbf{rem}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing.\textquotedblright{} Two languages, same move: the word for \emph{thing} collapses into the word for \emph{nothing}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the courtesy pair}]
\emph{gracias} $\to$ \emph{de nada} is a fixed \textbf{adjacency pair}: one turn expects the other. Learn them as a unit, the way English glues \emph{thank you} $\to$ \emph{you're welcome}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gracias\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}de nada\textquotedblright{} — the full exchange, both voices
  \item \textquotedblleft{}de nada\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}native, nature, natal\textquotedblright{} — nada's true family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{nada} (\textquotedblleft{}nothing\textquotedblright{}) started life as the Latin word for a \emph{born} — what? (A \emph{thing} — \emph{rēs nāta}, a born thing.) What English words share that \textquotedblleft{}born\textquotedblright{} root? (Native, nature, natal, renaissance.) Next: the verb the whole \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} question turns on — \textbf{estar}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Thank you, yes, and no — putting it together}

\label{lesson:ES-C04-repaso-gracias}



\begin{quote}
Two words that travel everywhere together. Nothing new in this lesson — only what you already have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Gracias.} — \textbf{De nada.}
\end{quote}

And the two words that let you answer anything at all:

\begin{quote}
— ¿…? — \textbf{Sí.}   /   — \textbf{No.}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can thank someone, answer when you are thanked, and — for the first time — accept or decline. Until you have \emph{sí} and \emph{no}, every question anyone asks you is unanswerable.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both parts, without stopping
  \item it again, faster, and let it sound like speech rather than recital
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run it once more from memory. If a word does not come, go back one lesson rather than pushing on — this chapter is short on purpose.
\end{tcolorbox}
